title: HOLDING ON
subtitle: A Freedwoman in the Black Belt, 1865–1877
introBody: Summer, 1865. The war is over and you are free — on paper. But the planter still owns the land, the county sheriff enforces the new Black Codes, and the Freedmen's Bureau agent in town may be gone before harvest. You have your children, a kitchen garden, and very little else. Every choice from here is yours to make.
trailFeedOpener: Summer 1865: emancipation reached the quarters last month, and already the planter is talking about contracts.

events.title: First autumn after emancipation — the Bureau agent comes to the quarters before the harvest contract deadline
events.text: The Freedmen's Bureau agent sits at a pine table in the yard, a ledger open in front of him. He tells you he can write your name and your children's names into a labor contract with the planter — wages set low, movement restricted to the county, but your family listed as contracted persons, not vagrants. He says the Black Codes are already being enforced two counties over. He also says, quieter, that he does not know how much longer the Bureau will have soldiers to back these papers up. Your eldest daughter is watching from the doorway. The planter is watching from the fence.

choices.text: You take the pen. You make your mark beside your name. The agent writes your children's names beneath yours.
choices.result: She chose to exist on paper — to let the diminishing machinery of federal protection hold her family's names, accepting that a contract is also a cage, because she judged that being named in any ledger was better than being named in none

choices.text: You tell the agent your labor is not his to record. You leave the table without signing.
choices.result: She refused legibility — she would not let survival require her to hand her family's names to a system she did not trust, accepting the exposure of unrecorded freedom rather than the partial shelter of a document she could not enforce

events.title: The Planter Wants the Garden Ground
events.text: The planter rides up and says the quarter-acre behind the cabin is his land and he needs it for cotton. Your kitchen garden — the sweet potatoes, the dried beans — is in it. He will let you keep it for a fee deducted from future wages.

choices.text: Pay the fee. Keep the garden.
choices.result: The sweet potatoes are safe through winter. Your youngest stops asking about supper twice a night.

choices.text: Refuse. Take the dispute to the Bureau agent.
choices.result: The agent writes a note but cannot force the planter's hand. The garden is plowed under while you wait. Neighbors remember you stood your ground.

choices.text: Quietly share the garden with two neighboring families.
choices.result: Three families tend it together now. The planter grumbles but does not move against all of you at once. Your children eat a little less so others can eat too.

image.artist: State Library and Archives of Florida

events.title: The Bureau Opens a School
events.text: The Freedmen's Bureau has set up a schoolroom in the church two miles off. Classes are in the morning — the same hours the planter expects your eldest daughter in the field. He says she misses school or she misses wages.

choices.text: Send her to school. Absorb the lost wages.
choices.result: She comes home spelling her name in the dirt by lamplight. You watch her and say nothing out loud.

choices.text: Keep her in the field this season, school next year.
choices.result: She does not argue. But she does not look at you the same way either.

choices.text: Ask the Bureau teacher to come evenings instead.
choices.result: The teacher agrees. Three other children from the quarters join. The planter cannot complain about evenings.

events.title: Vagrancy Patrol on the Road
events.text: You are walking to the crossroads market with a basket of preserves when two men on horses block the road. One wears a constable's badge. He says any colored person without proof of a labor contract can be arrested for vagrancy right now.

choices.text: Show your Bureau labor papers and stand firm.
choices.result: He reads the paper slowly, hands it back without a word, and rides on. Your hands stop shaking after a quarter mile.

choices.text: Pay him to look the other way.
choices.result: He pockets the coins and moves on. You make it to market. You do not tell anyone what it cost.

choices.text: Turn back. Not worth the risk today.
choices.result: You lose the sale and the walk home is long. The preserves will keep, but the money you needed will not come from nowhere.

events.title: The Church Meeting
events.text: The congregation is raising money to buy land and build a proper schoolhouse. The deacon asks every family to give what they can. It is more than you have easily — but you know what a church-owned school means for the children who come after yours.

choices.text: Give generously — more than you can spare.
choices.result: The deacon writes your name in the ledger first. Your children go to bed hungry two nights that week, and you do not regret it.
No one marks it either way. The fund grows slowly and so does the building.

choices.text: Offer labor instead of money — help build it.
choices.result: You spend three Saturdays hauling timber. Your daughter swings a hammer beside you. The schoolhouse goes up.

events.title: The County Court and the Apprenticeship Order
events.text: A county judge has signed an apprenticeship order for your youngest son — a Black Code clause that lets courts bind children of freedpeople to white households as unpaid labor. The sheriff will collect him in three days unless you can get the Bureau agent to block the order.

choices.text: Ride to the Bureau office immediately. Fight it legally.
choices.result: The agent files a counter-order. It takes ten days and two trips. Your son stays home. The planter is furious and docks your next wages on a pretext.

choices.text: Send your son to stay with kin in the next county quietly.
choices.result: He is safe but gone. You will not see him again until the order expires. You tell no one where he went.

choices.text: Accept the order. You cannot afford the fight.
choices.result: He is taken on a Tuesday morning. The wages you needed come, and they taste like nothing. Your daughter does not speak at supper for a week.

events.title: Crossroads Market Day
events.text: The Saturday market is busy. You have a basket of garden produce and some preserved goods. Each trip to a new customer is another chance — but a constable is making slow rounds, and the longer you stay the more attention you attract.
events.leaveText: Pack up and head home. Better safe.

attempts.buttonText: Sell to the nearest family quickly.
attempts.successText: A quick sale — fair price, no trouble. Coins in your apron.
attempts.failureText: The buyer haggles past patience. You sell low just to move on.

attempts.buttonText: Work the far end of the market for better prices.
attempts.successText: A freedman family pays well for the preserves. Good sale.
attempts.failureText: Constable stops you and demands to see your contract papers. You lose an hour and sell nothing else.

attempts.successText: Every jar gone. Best market day you've had.
attempts.failureText: Constable cites you for 'unlicensed trade.' You pay a fine or argue and get nothing either way.

events.title: Winter — a county sheriff and two men ride into the quarters demanding to see labor papers

text.default: You produce the contract. The agent's handwriting is faded but legible. The sheriff reads it, looks at you, looks at your children. He says something to the men with him that you cannot hear. They ride on. The paper worked, this time. You do not know whether the agent who wrote it still has a post, or whether the next sheriff will read it the same way. You hold the document after they leave and you cannot tell whether what you feel is protection or its performance.

variants.text: You produce the contract. The agent's handwriting is faded but legible. The sheriff reads it, looks at you, looks at your children. He says something to the men with him that you cannot hear. They ride on. The paper worked, this time. You do not know whether the agent who wrote it still has a post, or whether the next sheriff will read it the same way. You hold the document after they leave and you cannot tell whether what you feel is protection or its performance.

You have nothing to show them. The sheriff calls you vagrant by name — your name, which means someone told him. He says your youngest, being unbound, can be apprenticed to a tradesman under the county ordinance, for her own welfare. You stand between him and the door. You are calculating, in the space of a breath, what you have that is worth more than what you are about to lose, and whether there is anything you can do with your body right now that changes the answer. There is no Bureau agent within a day's ride.

events.title: Spring — word comes that the Bureau is closing its county office; the agent is leaving

text.default: The agent comes to tell you himself. He says the contract still carries legal weight in theory, that you can present it to a magistrate. You ask him which magistrate. He does not answer. The paper in your hands is the same paper it was in autumn. The world it was written inside has since dissolved, and the paper did not dissolve with it — but you are no longer sure what the paper is for, now that no one will stand behind it.

variants.text: The agent comes to tell you himself. He says the contract still carries legal weight in theory, that you can present it to a magistrate. You ask him which magistrate. He does not answer. The paper in your hands is the same paper it was in autumn. The world it was written inside has since dissolved, and the paper did not dissolve with it — but you are no longer sure what the paper is for, now that no one will stand behind it.

When the agent comes through to say goodbye you watch him from across the yard and do not walk over. Your family's names are in no ledger he is taking with him, and no ledger he is leaving behind. You have survived the winter by other means — by knowing which neighbors could be trusted, which roads the patrols avoided, what debts the planter believed he was owed and how to let him believe it a little longer. The Bureau is leaving. What you built without it remains, for now, because it was never built on the Bureau.

sages.name: Oliver Otis Howard
sages.title: Commissioner, Freedmen's Bureau
sages.bio: Oliver Otis Howard commanded the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands from its founding in 1865. He tried to use federal authority to enforce labor contracts, establish schools, and distribute land — but Congress limited his budget and President Johnson blocked land redistribution.
sages.greeting: The Bureau agent brings a letter from Washington. Commissioner Howard has written to every county office reminding agents that freedpeople's contracts must be registered and their terms witnessed.
sages.advice: The letter says Bureau agents are ordered to void any contract that does not specify wages in cash. It also says the Bureau's appropriations are uncertain after this session. Read between the lines: get your paperwork while you still can.

question.question: What was the Freedmen's Bureau primarily responsible for after the Civil War?
choices: Collecting taxes from Southern planters
Overseeing labor contracts, establishing schools, and protecting freedpeople's legal rights
Distributing weapons to Union veterans settling in the South
Supervising elections in Northern states
question.explanation: The Bureau negotiated labor contracts, set up schools and hospitals, and tried to enforce freedpeople's legal rights in Southern courts. Its authority was always limited by underfunding and presidential hostility.
question.teksRef: TEKS 8.9 — Reconstruction: promise of federal protection through the Freedmen's Bureau

sages.name: Blanche Kelso Bruce
sages.title: Educator, Planter, and Future U.S. Senator
sages.bio: Blanche Kelso Bruce was born enslaved in Virginia and escaped north before the war. He returned to Mississippi during Reconstruction, established a plantation, ran a school, served as a county sheriff and tax collector, and in 1875 was elected to the U.S. Senate — the first Black senator to serve a full term.
sages.greeting: A well-dressed Black man stops at the church door after Sunday services. He introduces himself as B.K. Bruce, asks how the school fund is going, and sits down to talk.
sages.advice: He says the vote is the foundation everything else rests on. 'They can dock your wages and burn your school,' he says, 'but a senator's vote is harder to take.' He means it as hope, not comfort.

question.question: How were Black men able to vote and hold office during Reconstruction?
choices: Southern states voluntarily extended voting rights as a condition of surrender
The Fifteenth Amendment and federal enforcement protected Black male suffrage
Only freedmen who had served in the Union Army were permitted to vote
Black voting rights applied only in states that had not seceded
question.explanation: The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) prohibited denying the vote based on race. Federal troops and Enforcement Acts backed it up during Radical Reconstruction, allowing Black men to vote and hold office — gains that collapsed when federal protection was withdrawn.
question.teksRef: TEKS 8.9 — Reconstruction: political gains of freedpeople and the role of the Fifteenth Amendment

sages.name: Thaddeus Stevens
sages.title: Radical Republican Congressman
sages.bio: Thaddeus Stevens was the floor leader for Radical Republican Reconstruction in the House. He pushed for land redistribution — 'forty acres' for freedpeople — and championed the Fourteenth Amendment. He died in 1868, and with him went the strongest congressional voice for genuine economic transformation in the South.
sages.greeting: The newspaper the Bureau agent leaves behind carries a speech by a Pennsylvania congressman named Stevens. The agent reads it aloud to the small crowd gathered on the porch.
sages.advice: Stevens argued that without land, freedom is only a word — the planter keeps all the leverage and the freedperson keeps all the risk. The speech is two years old now and Stevens is dead. But the argument still sits in the air.

question.question: What did Radical Republicans like Thaddeus Stevens argue freedpeople needed most to make emancipation real?
choices: Passage back to Africa funded by Congress
Access to land so they could support themselves independently of former planters
Immediate readmission of Southern states to restore order
A permanent standing army stationed in Washington
question.explanation: Stevens and other Radicals argued that land redistribution — famously 'forty acres' — was essential. Without land, freed people remained economically dependent on the same planters who had enslaved them, making genuine freedom impossible. Congress never passed large-scale land redistribution.
question.teksRef: TEKS 8.9 — Reconstruction: Radical Republican goals and the limits of federal action

route.title: Black Belt County, 1865–1877
route.description: You remain here — on this land, in this county — navigating each year as it comes.

eventTrivia.question: What were the Black Codes?
choices: Laws passed by Congress to protect freedpeople's rights
Southern state laws that restricted the freedom of formerly enslaved people
Secret rules enforced by the Freedmen's Bureau
eventTrivia.fact: Southern states passed Black Codes immediately after the war to control freedpeople's labor, movement, and legal rights — effectively recreating many conditions of slavery.

eventTrivia.question: What could happen to a freedperson arrested under a vagrancy law?
choices: They could be fined or forced into unpaid labor for a white employer
They were sent north by the Freedmen's Bureau
They received a cash payment and a new contract
eventTrivia.fact: Vagrancy laws made it illegal to be unemployed or without a labor contract. Those arrested could be fined and, if unable to pay, leased as forced labor — a form of re-enslavement.

eventTrivia.question: Why did apprenticeship clauses in Black Codes concern freedpeople?
choices: They required children to attend Bureau schools
They allowed courts to bind Black children to white households as unpaid workers
They gave planters the right to buy land at low prices
eventTrivia.fact: Apprenticeship clauses let county courts remove children from freedpeople's families and bind them as unpaid laborers to white employers — separating families as slavery had done.

eventTrivia.question: What was one major goal of Freedmen's Bureau schools?
choices: Training freedpeople to return to skilled trades in Northern cities
Teaching literacy so freedpeople could read contracts, laws, and ballots
Preparing freedpeople to serve in the U.S. military
eventTrivia.fact: Literacy was a form of power. Freedpeople who could read their own labor contracts were harder to cheat; those who could read ballots could exercise political rights. Planters often opposed Bureau schools for exactly this reason.

eventTrivia.question: Why did many freedpeople distrust labor contracts even when the Bureau witnessed them?
choices: The contracts were written in French and hard to read
Planters often docked wages on pretexts or refused to pay at year's end
The Bureau required all contracts to be renewed every week
eventTrivia.fact: Even Bureau-witnessed contracts could be undermined. Planters charged inflated commissary prices, invented 'damages,' or simply refused to pay — and freedpeople had little legal recourse once the harvest was in.

eventTrivia.question: What amendment abolished slavery throughout the United States?
choices: The Thirteenth Amendment
The Fourteenth Amendment
The Fifteenth Amendment
eventTrivia.fact: The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in December 1865, abolished slavery and involuntary servitude except as punishment for a crime — the constitutional foundation of emancipation.

eventTrivia.question: What did the Fourteenth Amendment guarantee?
choices: The right of Black men to vote
Equal citizenship and equal protection of the laws for all persons born in the United States
Land grants of forty acres to every freedman
eventTrivia.fact: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) made all persons born in the U.S. citizens and guaranteed equal protection — directly targeting Black Codes that treated freedpeople as second-class persons.

eventTrivia.question: What was the Compromise of 1877's main effect on Reconstruction?
choices: It extended the Freedmen's Bureau's funding for ten more years
It resulted in federal troops being withdrawn from the South, ending Reconstruction
It gave Southern states new land to distribute to freedpeople
eventTrivia.fact: The disputed 1876 election was resolved when Republicans agreed to withdraw federal troops from the South. Without military enforcement, Reconstruction governments fell and freedpeople lost the federal protection that had backed their rights.

eventTrivia.question: How did the KKK undermine Reconstruction?
choices: By lobbying Congress to reduce Bureau funding
By terrorizing Black voters, officeholders, and Bureau agents to suppress political participation
By organizing labor strikes on Southern plantations
eventTrivia.fact: The Ku Klux Klan used murder, arson, and beating to drive Black voters away from polls and force Black officeholders out. The Enforcement Acts of 1870–71 temporarily suppressed the Klan but could not end the underlying violence.

eventTrivia.question: Why did Black churches become central institutions during Reconstruction?
choices: The federal government required freedpeople to worship in separate buildings
Churches provided community meeting space, schools, and mutual aid outside white control
Planters funded church construction to keep freedpeople occupied on Sundays
eventTrivia.fact: Black churches were often the only institutions freedpeople fully controlled. They housed schools, hosted political meetings, organized mutual aid, and preserved community ties — making them targets of Klan violence.

eventTrivia.question: What was sharecropping, and why was it often called a 'new form of bondage'?
choices: A system where freedpeople rented land and paid with a share of the crop, but debt kept them permanently tied to the planter's land
A government program that gave freedpeople a share of abandoned plantation land
A railroad scheme that hired freedpeople to lay track in exchange for farm plots
eventTrivia.fact: Sharecroppers paid rent with a portion of their harvest, but planters controlled the accounting. Inflated supply costs and manipulated ledgers left most sharecroppers in permanent debt — legally binding them to the land much as slavery had.

eventTrivia.question: What did Radical Republicans in Congress do to take control of Reconstruction away from President Johnson?
choices: They impeached Johnson and replaced him with Ulysses Grant immediately
They passed the Reconstruction Acts of 1867, dividing the South into military districts with new voter registration requirements
They dissolved the Supreme Court and rewrote the Constitution
eventTrivia.fact: The Reconstruction Acts of 1867 placed Southern states under military rule and required them to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment and allow Black male suffrage before rejoining the Union — bypassing Johnson's lenient Presidential Reconstruction.

eventTrivia.question: What happened to the Freedmen's Bureau by the early 1870s?
choices: It expanded into a permanent federal civil rights agency
Congress ended most of its functions, leaving freedpeople without federal enforcement of labor contracts
It was transferred to state governments in the South to run locally
eventTrivia.fact: Congress steadily cut the Bureau's budget and authority. By 1872 most operations had ended. Freedpeople who had relied on Bureau agents to witness contracts and hear grievances were left without recourse.

eventTrivia.question: Why was literacy so threatening to planters and Black Code legislators?
choices: Literate freedpeople could communicate with foreign governments
It allowed freedpeople to read contracts, laws, and newspapers — and to organize politically
Planters feared literate workers would leave farming for city jobs immediately
eventTrivia.fact: A freedperson who could read a contract could catch fraudulent clauses; one who could read a newspaper could follow political events; one who could write could correspond with lawyers, Bureau agents, and allies. Planters understood literacy as a transfer of power.

eventTrivia.question: What was President Andrew Johnson's approach to Reconstruction, and how did it differ from the Radical Republicans?
choices: Johnson wanted to punish Southern states severely; Radicals wanted quick readmission
Johnson wanted quick, lenient readmission with few protections for freedpeople; Radicals demanded civil rights guarantees before readmission
Johnson and the Radicals agreed on all major Reconstruction policies
eventTrivia.fact: Johnson's Presidential Reconstruction restored Southern states quickly and allowed them to pass Black Codes. Radical Republicans in Congress overrode him, passing the Reconstruction Acts and the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments over his vetoes.

eventTrivia.question: What was one genuine political achievement of Reconstruction that was later reversed?
choices: Black men voting and serving in state legislatures and the U.S. Congress
A permanent federal guarantee of forty acres of land to every freedman
The abolition of the plantation system throughout the South
eventTrivia.fact: During Reconstruction, over 2,000 Black men held public office, including senators, congressmen, judges, and sheriffs. These gains were systematically stripped away after 1877 through violence, literacy tests, poll taxes, and new state constitutions.

historicalContext: Between 1865 and 1877, four million formerly enslaved people navigated a world that offered emancipation on paper and re-bondage in practice. Black Codes, vagrancy laws, and apprenticeship clauses rebuilt white supremacy through law. The Freedmen's Bureau, the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, and Radical Republican congresses offered real but fragile protections. When federal troops withdrew in 1877, Reconstruction's promises collapsed into sharecropping, convict leasing, and Jim Crow. The women and men who lived through it built churches, schools, families, and communities under conditions designed to prevent exactly that.

family.default: Your family remembers you as someone who tried to hold them together against everything that pulled at the seams.

variants.text: Your children carry your name like something worth carrying. They know you chose them, again and again, even when it cost you. They will tell their own children what you did.
Your family knows you did what you could. Some choices still sit between you and them unspoken. They love you and they remember the hardness alongside the warmth.
The distance between you and your children was built one choice at a time. They understand survival. They are not sure it required all of what it cost them.

community.default: The people around you remember you as someone who was present in the hard years.

variants.text: The church women say your name when they talk about who built something lasting here. You gave when giving was hard, and the school and the congregation stand partly on that.
People in the quarters remember you as a neighbor — present, careful, neither first nor last when it mattered. You kept your own counsel, and most understand why.
You survived by keeping to yourself, and the community felt it. They do not blame you for the weight you carried, but they remember who was absent when the common cause needed bodies.
